docs.title: Active Directory (AD) والـ Kerberos Protocol Attacks
Active Directory (AD) والـ Kerberos Protocol Attacks
docs.text:
مش حوار CVE جديد بس موضوع مهم اوي في ال cyber security وهو ال Active Directory (AD) والـ Attacks بتاعته بالتحديد Kerberos Protocol

لقيته مهم فا حبيت اختصره و افيدكم

docs.title: مقدمة عن الـ AD
docs.text:
ممكن نشرح شرح بسيط لاي الAD

وهو إن أي شركه بيكون لها سيستم اكونتات مرتبطه مع بعض تحت مسمى الدومين، بيتوزع منه اكونتات لكل موظف في الشركه

والAD مسؤول من تاكد ان الاكونت دا تبع الدومين ولا لا

العملية دي اسمها AD انما الجهاز المسؤول عن الكلام دا هو ال Domain Controller (DC)

طيب الAD عمليه بتنقسم لجزئين:

  • السيستم بتاع الDC
  • والعمليه بتاع التحقق نفسها (Authentication)

docs.title: عملية الـ Authentication
docs.text:
طيب DC System نسيبه شويه عشان نركز على اليوزر عشان هو سبب خراب كل شيء

(اقصد يعني هو المستهدف من الAttacker يعني اخي اليوزر)

اولا هنتكلم عن ال default اي الي بيحصل:

اليوزر بيسجل على الاكونت باليوزر وكلمه السر بيبعت للDC عشان يسمحله فا بيبعت حاجه اسمها AS-REQ

الريكوست دا عباره عن الtimestamp الي هو الوقت يعني بهاش باسورد الاكونت بتاعه (بنسميه NT HASH)

الDC بـ decrypt الكلام دا ويتاكد منه اه دا يوزر عندي على الدومين ويقوم باعت حاجه اسمها الـ TGT تيكت فيها بيانات اليوزر والصلاحيه متشفره بهاش باسورد اكونت الدومين اسمه KRBTGT مع session key يستخدمها لتشفير الاتصال

طيب انا عايز Access على داتا بيز في سيرفر او اي خدمه عموما؟

لازم نطلب من الDC تحقق تاني عشان يسمحلنا نستخدم الخدمه، افرض انا مليش صلاحيه؟

ببعتله تاني الTGT بقوله انا تم التحقق مني قبل كدا ممكن ادخل الداتا بيز؟ (مع SPN اسم الخدمه)

يـ decrypt التيكت ويتاكد ان كل حاجه تمام ومسموحه، يبعتله تيكت اسمها TGS عباره عن بيانات الصلاحية متشفره بهاش باسورد اكونت السيرفس ايا كانت ويروح بيها للسيرفس يأكسس عليها، المثال هنا الداتا بيز

docs.title: بسم الله نبدأ في الـ Attacks
docs.text:
هقولك دلوقتي: لو انا جبت الTGT أو TGS بطريقه ما علطول بدون كل البروسيس دي وانا اصلا مش اليوزر صاحب التيكت (attacker) واستخدمته وعملت اكسيس بالتيكت او كملت البروسيس بيها؟

دا اسمه:Pass the Ticket (PtT) Attack

طب انا يوزر عادي (اتهكر) و عايز ادخل الداتا بيز ومليش صلاحيه

جبت هاش باسورد يوزر (lateral movement) تاني له صلاحيه وعملت طلب AS-REQ

هيرجعلي TGT واكمل لحد ما اوصل access؟

دا:Overpass the Hash Attack

طيب لو Privilege Escalation ووصلت لدومين ادمن اكونت وجبت هاش krbtgt هتعمل TGT براحتك

دا:Golden Ticket Attack

طب انت هكرت يوزر ومعاك هاش باسورد اكونت الخدمه بطريقه ما؟

دا:Silver Ticket Attack

طب انت مش معاك الهاش دا تجيبه ازاي؟

انت Attacker على جهاز يوزر تستنى يطلب تيكت TGS

وبعدين تجيبه Memo Dump (نسخه من الذاكره) وتجيب الهاش تفكه عشان تعرف باسورد اكونت الخدمه عشان تعمل Silver Ticket Attack؟

دا:Kerberoasting Attack

docs.title: ندخل على ال Defense؟
docs.text:
التسلسل الطبيعي لل event id للـ process بتاعه التحقق من الاكونت:

[DC: 4768]     ──(إصدار TGT)
[DC: 4769]     ──(إصدار TGS)
[Target: 4624] ──(Access Granted)

و [Target: 4625] لو اليوزر غلط في كلمه السر ولا حاجه

لقيتهم بعيد عن بعض في الوقت، لقيت ان في event id ناقص في حاجه غريبه، ابدأ Investigate بقا عشان ممكن يكون في Attack من الي فوق

وبس كدا

ان أصبت فهو من عند الله وان اخطأت فهو من نفسي والشيطان :)

docs.title: Active Directory (AD) and Kerberos Protocol Attacks
Active Directory (AD) and Kerberos Protocol Attacks
docs.text:
🇪🇬 اقرأ بالعربي

Not a new CVE discussion, but something important in cyber security: Active Directory (AD) and its attacks, specifically the Kerberos Protocol.

I found it important, so I wanted to summarize it and share the benefit.

docs.title: Intro to AD
docs.text:
Let's give a simple explanation of what AD is.

Any company has a system of accounts linked together under something called the domain, and from it accounts are distributed to every employee in the company.

AD is responsible for making sure that account actually belongs to the domain or not.

This process is called AD, but the machine responsible for handling it is the Domain Controller (DC).

AD as a process is split into two parts:

  • The DC system itself
  • The authentication process itself

docs.title: The Authentication Process
docs.text:
Let's set the DC system aside a bit and focus on the user, since the user is the reason everything falls apart

(I mean, the user is the target of the Attacker — basically, my brother, the user).

First, let's talk about the default, i.e. what normally happens:

The user logs into the account with the username and password, which gets sent to the DC so it authorizes him, so he sends something called AS-REQ.

This request is basically the timestamp — meaning the time — encrypted with the hash of the account's password (we call it the NT HASH).

The DC decrypts this and confirms, "yes, this is a user I have on the domain," and sends back something called the TGT — a ticket containing the user's data and privileges, encrypted with the hash of the domain account's password called KRBTGT, along with a session key used to encrypt the connection.

Now, say I want Access to a database on a server, or any service in general?

I need to ask the DC to authenticate again so it lets me use the service — suppose I don't have permission?

I send it the TGT again, saying "I've already been authenticated before, can I access the database?" (along with the SPN, the service name).

It decrypts the ticket and confirms everything is fine and allowed, and sends back a ticket called TGS — containing the privilege data, encrypted with the hash of the service account's password, whatever that service is — and I go use it to access the service, in this example, the database.

docs.title: Bismillah, let's start on the Attacks
docs.text:
Here's the thing now: if I got the TGT or TGS somehow, straight up, without going through all that process — and I'm not actually the user who owns the ticket (attacker) — and I used it and gained access with the ticket, or completed the process using it?

This is called:Pass the Ticket (PtT) Attack

Okay, so I'm a regular user (got hacked) and I want to get into the database and I have no permission.

I got the password hash of another user (lateral movement) who does have permission, and sent an AS-REQ request.

It'll give me back a TGT and I continue until I get access?

This is:Overpass the Hash Attack

Now, if there's Privilege Escalation and I reach a domain admin account and get the krbtgt hash, I can make a TGT freely, whenever I want.

This is:Golden Ticket Attack

Okay, so you hacked a user and somehow have the hash of the service account's password?

This is:Silver Ticket Attack

But if you don't have that hash, how do you get it?

You're an Attacker on a user's machine, waiting for him to request a TGS ticket

Then you grab it via Memory Dump (a copy of memory) and get the hash, then crack it to find out the service account's password so you can carry out a Silver Ticket Attack?

This is:Kerberoasting Attack

docs.title: Let's get into Defense
docs.text:
The normal sequence of event IDs for the account authentication process:

[DC: 4768]     ──(TGT issued)
[DC: 4769]     ──(TGS issued)
[Target: 4624] ──(Access Granted)

And [Target: 4625] if the user gets the password wrong or something.

If you find them spread far apart in time, or you find that some event ID is missing — something's off — start Investigating, because there could be an Attack from the ones mentioned above.

And that's it.

If I got it right, it's from God, and if I made a mistake, it's from myself and Satan :)

docs.title: CVE-2015–0311, use-after-free vulnerability in Adobe Flash Player, exploited (Qadars banking Trojan)
CVE-2015–0311, use-after-free vulnerability in Adobe Flash Player, exploited (Qadars banking Trojan)
docs.text: CVE-2015–0311: A Deep Dive into Adobe Flash’s Critical Use-After-Free Vulnerability

docs.title: A cybersecurity analysis of one of the most notorious zero-day exploits
docs.text: بسم الله المعين Let’s talk about CVE-2015–0311. Back in 2015, Adobe published information about a zero-day critical use-after-free vulnerability that shook the cybersecurity world.

docs.title: The Technical Foundation
docs.text: The story begins with Adobe Flash Player — a program that allows you to open files loaded on your device. Any files processed through Adobe Flash were obfuscated using a tool called SecureSWF from Adobe.

docs.title: How the Vulnerability Works
docs.text:
With every file operation, there are compression & decompression processes happening behind the scenes. When you open a specific file, the system starts to decompress the ByteArray — which is the object that Adobe uses for binary data (files and other data we're working with).

This process is dynamically resized through a function in a library called zlib with a script running on Adobe’s ActionScript Virtual Machine. During decompression, the buffer of this object increases in memory.

Here’s where it gets interesting: an object called the Subscriber notifies other objects working with addresses about the new pointers that the applicationDomainmemory function changed to new locations. When everything goes right, this process completes successfully.

docs.title: Where Things Go Wrong
docs.text:
But what happens when decompression fails? Say the file is corrupted, for example.

A function called inflate in zlib alerts a memory function called UncompressViaZlibVariant, which performs a rollback by freeing the memory that was added to the buffer — essentially returning everything back to its original state.

Here’s the critical vulnerability: applicationDomainmemory leaves the pointers to the freed buffer — the empty space that was deleted! The subscriber doesn't notify that the data failed and everything should return to its original place.

You now have a hole in memory without anyone knowing about it. Combined with SecureSWF’s obfuscation capabilities, this becomes the perfect staging ground for malware :)

docs.title: Delivery Method
docs.text:
Attackers used phishing emails as their primary delivery method. Those who created exploits for this CVE utilized Angler EK — an exploit kit that became notorious in the cybercriminal underworld.

The attack flow worked like this:

  1. Attacker rents a domain
  2. Uses the toolkit to redirect victims to a malicious page
  3. The page scans the user’s OS to identify available zero-days
  4. Serves the user a malicious file tailored to their vulnerabilities

docs.title: The Qadars Banking Trojan
docs.text: The most infamous malware that leveraged this vulnerability was the Qadars banking Trojan. What made this malware particularly sophisticated was its multiple anti-analysis techniques.

docs.title: Advanced Evasion Techniques
docs.text:
Normally, imports in malware are somewhat visible through APIs, but Qadars took a different approach — all APIs were hashed.

But how does it resolve one-directional hashes? Here’s the clever part:

  1. Enumeration: It enumerates all DLLs on your system
  2. Resolution: Identifies which API belongs to which DLL and resolves it in the table
  3. Concealment: Prevents you from seeing these operations

docs.title: Triple XOR Encoding
docs.text:
The sophistication doesn’t stop there. Before calling any API and performing resolution, everything gets encoded with a 4-byte key XOR:

  • First XOR: Before making the call
  • Second XOR: After making the call (same key)
  • Third XOR: After resolution in the table (same key again)

This makes memory snapshots nearly useless for analysis — a nightmare for security researchers.

docs.title: Backup Social Engineering
docs.text: Even if the Use-After-Free exploit failed, Qadars had a fallback plan. It would display a fake update page for either Adobe or Windows. Once users granted administrative privileges thinking they were installing a legitimate update, the malware could complete its mission through social engineering rather than technical exploitation.

docs.title: Adobe’s Response
docs.text: Beyond Adobe’s immediate patch, the industry needed more robust defenses.

docs.title: Control Flow Guard (CFG)
docs.text:
With Windows 8.1 and later versions, Microsoft introduced Control Flow Guard (CFG). This mitigation works by:

  1. Pre-check verification: Before any use of a specific memory location, it checks a table of addresses that will be used
  2. Safety flagging: Sets a flag indicating the location is safe
  3. Process termination: If there’s any use or indirect call to an external pointer without a proper flag, it terminates the process immediately

This effectively neutralizes many use-after-free exploits by preventing unauthorized memory access.

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
CVE-2015–0311 represents a perfect storm of technical sophistication and social engineering. It demonstrates how attackers combine:

  • Technical vulnerabilities (use-after-free)
  • Advanced evasion (multiple XOR encoding, API hashing)
  • Social engineering (fake update pages)
  • Infrastructure (exploit kits, rented domains)

And that’s it!

If I did well, it’s from Allah, and if I erred, it’s from myself and demon :)

docs.title: BlackLotus UEFI Bootkit: A Deep Dive into CVE-2022–21849
BlackLotus UEFI Bootkit: A Deep Dive into CVE-2022–21849
docs.text:
The world of cybersecurity is constantly evolving, and with each new advancement, attackers develop more sophisticated techniques to bypass security measures. One of the most dangerous threats in recent years is BlackLotus, a UEFI bootkit that exploits CVE-2022–21849 to compromise Windows 11 at the firmware level.

This attack is particularly stealthy and persistent, meaning that even if you format your hard drive or reinstall your OS, the malware remains active. In this deep dive, we’ll explore:

✅ How UEFI bootkits work ✅ The infection process of BlackLotus ✅ Why it is nearly impossible to remove ✅ How it bypasses Secure Boot and antivirus tools ✅ Mitigation techniques to protect against it

docs.title: 🚀 What is BlackLotus?
docs.text:
BlackLotus is a UEFI bootkit — a form of firmware-level malware that infects the UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface), which is responsible for initializing hardware components and booting the OS.

Unlike traditional malware, UEFI bootkits execute before the operating system even loads, giving them full control over the machine before security tools (such as antivirus or EDR solutions) can activate.

This level of control allows attackers to:

🔹 Disable security mechanisms like Secure Boot and Windows Defender 🔹 Bypass endpoint security solutions 🔹 Inject malware into the boot process to establish persistence 🔹 Modify system firmware to prevent removal

docs.title: 💡 A Quick Refresher on the Boot Process
docs.text:
To understand why BlackLotus is so dangerous, let’s quickly review how a system boots:

1️⃣ Power On — The motherboard supplies power, initializing system components. 2️⃣ Firmware Execution (UEFI/BIOS) — The system firmware (stored in non-volatile memory) checks and initializes hardware components. 3️⃣ Bootloader Execution — The firmware locates the bootloader (like Windows Boot Manager), which loads the OS kernel into memory. 4️⃣ OS Startup — The operating system fully loads, and security solutions like EDR/antivirus tools start running.

If an attacker can modify the firmware stage, they gain full control over the entire boot process before any security mechanism can detect them.

This is exactly what BlackLotus does.

docs.title: 🔎 The Story Behind BlackLotus & CVE-2022–21849
docs.text:
BlackLotus is an evolution of an older UEFI bootkit attack called MonoBounce.

🔹 MonoBounce Attack — An early UEFI-based attack that modified the UEFI startup sequence to inject malicious code. However, once detected, security patches prevented further exploitation.

🔹 BlackLotus took it further by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2022–21849) to bypass Microsoft’s Secure Boot protections and embed itself deep inside the firmware.

docs.title: 🛠 How Does BlackLotus Infect a System?
docs.text:
BlackLotus is typically delivered via:

✔️ Phishing emails containing malicious attachments ✔️ Drive-by downloads from compromised websites ✔️ Trojanized software posing as legitimate tools

Once executed, BlackLotus exploits a signed driver named RTCCore64.sys, which was originally designed for GPU configuration.

💡 Why Does Windows Trust It? The driver is legitimate and signed, meaning Windows does not treat it as a threat. Since this driver can modify hardware settings, it has kernel-level access — the highest level of privilege on the system.

💀 BlackLotus takes advantage of this to modify UEFI firmware.

docs.title: 🚨 What Happens After Infection?
docs.text:
Once BlackLotus is installed, it modifies several key components of the system:

🔴 EFI Boot Files — It injects malicious code into the UEFI firmware files. 🔴 Boot Configuration Data (BCD) — This is Windows’ boot configuration. If modified, Windows typically refuses to start — but BlackLotus alters it and its backup, preventing recovery. 🔴 Disables Secure Boot — Secure Boot is designed to prevent unauthorized code from running at startup. BlackLotus bypasses it completely.

This allows the attacker to inject malware at every boot, making it extremely difficult to remove.

docs.title: 🔄 Why Is It Impossible to Remove?
docs.text:
One of the most frightening aspects of BlackLotus is its persistence. Even if a victim:

✅ Formats the hard drive ✅ Reinstalls Windows ✅ Uses a fresh OS image

The malware survives.

docs.title: 🔍 How?
docs.text:
BlackLotus modifies the Machine Owner Key (MOK) stored in NVRAM (Non-Volatile RAM).

🔹 MOK (Machine Owner Key) — A security key that allows the system owner to control boot settings. 🔹 NVRAM (Non-Volatile RAM) — A special memory area that does not get wiped during OS reinstallation.

By modifying MOK, BlackLotus ensures that every new OS installation is compromised at boot.

docs.title: 👀 What Does BlackLotus Do After Boot?
docs.text:
Once the OS starts, BlackLotus ensures persistence and executes multiple payloads:

✔️ Injects malicious DLLs — Prevents security software from detecting it ✔️ Activates an HTTP downloader — Fetches additional malware like RATs, Trojans, and keyloggers ✔️ Establishes a C2 (Command & Control) server — Sends stolen data and receives attacker commands ✔️ Runs privilege escalation exploits — Gains full system access

Since the malware operates before the OS fully loads, traditional antivirus solutions are completely ineffective.

docs.title: 🛡 How Can You Protect Against BlackLotus?
docs.text: Because BlackLotus is so advanced, mitigation is difficult — but not impossible. Here’s what you can do:

docs.title: 1️⃣ Enable Full Secure Boot Enforcement
docs.text: Ensure Secure Boot is turned on and that revocation lists are up-to-date. Microsoft has released updates to block vulnerable bootloaders.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Disable Third-Party Key Enrollment
docs.text: Prevent unauthorized changes to the MOK in NVRAM.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Update Your Firmware
docs.text: Many manufacturers have released firmware updates that patch UEFI vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Use Advanced EDR Solutions
docs.text: Standard antivirus software cannot detect UEFI infections. Use firmware-level security tools that scan for malicious bootkits.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Monitor Boot Configuration Data (BCD)
docs.text: Regularly check for unexpected modifications to BCD files and Secure Boot settings.

docs.title: 🚀 Final Thoughts
docs.text:
BlackLotus is a game-changing malware that demonstrates the power and danger of UEFI bootkits. By bypassing Secure Boot, modifying firmware settings, and embedding itself into NVRAM, it achieves a level of persistence that is nearly impossible to remove.

Organizations and individuals must adopt firmware security best practices to prevent such stealthy, persistent threats from taking over their systems.

As UEFI-based attacks become more common, the need for hardware-level security solutions will only grow.

🛡 Stay vigilant. Security begins before the OS even loads.

docs.title: A Technical Analysis of a Destructive Cyber Campaign

The Shamoon malware, first identified in 2012 and reemerging in 2016 and 2018, represents a pinnacle of destructive cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure. This article provides a detailed technical analysis of the 2018 Shamoon 3 attack on a Saudi Arabian petroleum company, focusing on its execution, payload mechanics, and defensive strategies. Aimed at cybersecurity analysts, this guide includes commands for investigation and mitigation, offering actionable insights for both junior and senior professionals.
The Incident: A Coordinated Strike
docs.text: On December 10, 2018, a Saudi Arabian oil production company suffered a severe attack, with 42 devices rendered inoperable and a network of approximately 15,000 devices compromised. The attack culminated in the overwriting of the Master Boot Record (MBR), making systems unbootable. This was the result of a meticulously planned, low-and-slow campaign spanning months.

docs.title: October 9–11: Initial Access via Dormant Credentials
docs.text:
Attackers exploited active administrative accounts belonging to former employees, likely through phishing or credential reuse. These accounts provided domain-level access to the network.

Investigation Commands:

  • Check for active accounts of former employees:
Get-ADUser -Filter {Enabled -eq $true} -Properties LastLogonDate,Description | Where-Object {($_.Description -like "*terminated*") -or ($_.LastLogonDate -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-90))} | Select-Object Name,LastLogonDate
  • Review audit logs for suspicious logins:
Get-WinEvent -LogName "Security" | Where-Object {$_.Id -eq 4624 -and $_.Properties[5].Value -like "*admin*"} | Select-Object TimeCreated,@{Name="Account";Expression={$_.Properties[5].Value}}

docs.title: October 29–31: Lateral Movement and Target Selection
docs.text:
The attackers used PsExec for remote execution and attempted RDP brute force attacks to expand their foothold. Network discovery was conducted via SMB (Port 445) and ICMP scans to identify high-value targets.

Investigation Commands:

  • Detect PsExec usage in logs:
Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" | Where-Object {$_.Id -eq 1 -and $_.Message -like "*psexec*"} | Select-Object TimeCreated,@{Name="CommandLine";Expression={$_.Properties[10].Value}}
  • Identify SMB scanning activity:
Get-WinEvent -LogName "Security" | Where-Object {$_.Id -eq 445} | Select-Object TimeCreated,@{Name="SourceIP";Expression={$_.Properties[18].Value}}
  • Monitor ICMP traffic:
tshark -i eth0 -f "icmp" -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e ip.dst

docs.title: November 19: Command-and-Control via WinRM
docs.text:
Attackers leveraged Windows Remote Management (WinRM) to configure payloads and establish C2 communication with external servers.

Investigation Commands:

  • Check for WinRM activity:
Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational" | Where-Object {$_.Id -eq 91} | Select-Object TimeCreated,@{Name="ClientIP";Expression={$_.Properties[2].Value}}
  • List active WinRM listeners:
winrm enumerate winrm/config/listener

docs.title: December 10: MBR Overwrite
docs.text:
On December 10, a scheduled task triggered the Shamoon payload, overwriting the MBR on 42 devices, including servers. This rendered systems unbootable, halting operations.

Investigation Commands:

  • Identify scheduled tasks:
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {$_.State -eq "Ready"} | Select-Object TaskName,TaskPath,Date
  • Check for MBR modifications:
dd if=/dev/sda bs=512 count=1 | hexdump -C

docs.title: Why EDR Failed
docs.text:
Darktrace’s EDR detected PsExec, RDP brute force, and WinRM activity, but the attack succeeded due to:

Detection Without Action : Alerts were raised but not investigated by the security team.

Disabled Automation : Darktrace Antigena (autonomous response) was disabled during a trial.

Human Oversight : Manual response was required but not executed in time.

Low-and-Slow Approach : Gradual movement evaded detection thresholds.

Time-Triggered Payload : The payload executed at a preset time, bypassing real-time intervention.

docs.title: Malware Analysis: Inside ISM.exe
docs.text:
The payload included ISM.exe (565 KB), deployed during the WinRM phase for information gathering. It collected:

  • Antivirus and firewall products.
  • System date, time, and timezone.
  • Local domain and %username% (via systeminfo).
  • Running processes (via tasklist).
  • WPAD and proxy configurations.

Analysis Commands:

  • Extract system information:
systeminfo > system_info.txt
tasklist > process_list.txt
  • Check for ISM.exe:
Get-Process | Where-Object {$_.Path -like "*ISM.exe*"} | Select-Object Name,Path,StartTime

docs.title: Sabotage and Evasion
docs.text:
The malware executed:

Process Termination: Killed winit.exe to force shutdowns.

taskkill /IM winit.exe /F

Scheduled Tasks: Created tasks for persistence.

schtasks /create /tn "MaliciousTask" /tr "C:\malware.exe" /sc once /st 00:00

Disabled Defenses: Blocked Windows updates and checks.

net stop wuauserv

Communication Blocks: Disrupted DNS and HTTP to prevent alerts.

netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="BlockDNS" dir=out protocol=udp localport=53 action=block

Cleanup: Deleted temporary files.

del /q /s %TEMP%\*

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: The attack disrupted a critical petroleum company, destroying 42 devices and affecting a 15,000-device network. Recovery required extensive resources, impacting operations and finances.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Restore MBR:
  2. Reinstall OS: Use a clean image after network sanitization.
  3. Network Cleanup: Scan for residual malware.

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
1. Disable Unnecessary Services:
  2. Revoke Legacy Accounts:
  3. Enforce MFA:
  4. Monitor Lateral Movement:
  5. Enable Autonomous Response:
  6. Segment Network:

docs.title: Boot Process: Why MBR Matters
docs.text:
[Power Button]
      ↓
[Power Supply]
      ↓
[CPU → BIOS/UEFI]
      ↓
[POST: Hardware Check]
      ↓
[Boot Device]
      ↓
[MBR → Bootloader]   ← Shamoon Overwrites
      ↓
[Bootloader → Kernel]
      ↓
[Init → Desktop]

A corrupted MBR halts booting, requiring manual recovery.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. EDR requires active monitoring and response.
  2. Legacy accounts are high-risk entry points.
  3. Scheduled tasks are often overlooked.
  4. Low-and-slow attacks demand vigilant SOCs.
  5. Automation is essential for real-time defense.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: The Shamoon 3 attack exemplifies the devastating potential of targeted malware. By exploiting dormant accounts, leveraging legitimate tools, and executing a time-triggered payload, attackers crippled a critical organization. This analysis, complete with investigation and mitigation commands, underscores the need for proactive defenses, automated responses, and rigorous credential management. As threats evolve, defenders must stay one step ahead to protect critical infrastructure.

docs.title: CVE-2022–26134: The Confluence RCE That Shook Enterprise Security
CVE-2022–26134: The Confluence RCE That Shook Enterprise Security
A Deep Dive into the Critical Vulnerability That Exposed Thousands of Organizations
docs.text:
بسم الله المعين

Another conversation about Cyber Security before I disappear into graduation year — please keep me in your prayers for success! 👋🏻

docs.title: Today’s discussion might be a bit different because we’re stepping slightly away from the usual territory. We’re diving into the remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability that made waves in 2022: CVE-2022–26134, classified as High severity.
The Timeline: A Zero-Day Nightmare
docs.text:
In June 2022, Atlassian — the Australian software company behind popular tools like Trello — dropped a bombshell announcement. They disclosed a Zero-Day vulnerability in their Confluence platform (a content collaboration and file-sharing platform), and at that moment, there was no patch available.

The security community held its breath for exactly one day. Atlassian released emergency patches the very next day, and we all hoped that would be the end of it.

Spoiler alert: It wasn’t.

Rapid7 quickly announced that active exploitation had already begun, with attacks targeting numerous companies and their customers. The breach window was open, and attackers were rushing through.

docs.title: Understanding RCE: Remote Code Execution
docs.text:
First, let’s break down the acronym. RCE stands for Remote Code Execution — exactly what it sounds like, and just as dangerous.

In this case, the vulnerability allowed any attacker to send HTTP requests (GET, POST, etc.) to the Confluence Server or Data Center. These requests contained OGNL payloads that would execute on the server and return responses that clearly indicated successful code execution.

docs.title: What is OGNL?
docs.text:
OGNL (Object-Graph Navigation Language) is a Java-based expression language with a specific format that allows direct access to Java objects. The format looks like this:

${code}

The vulnerability existed because requests were passing user-controlled URIs directly to the OGNL parser. Anyone with Burp Suite (or similar tools) could exploit this attack vector with minimal effort.

docs.title: The Proof of Concept: How Attackers Confirmed the Vulnerability
docs.text:
To verify the vulnerability, attackers crafted requests that would return the execution result in the HTTP response through a custom header called X-Cmd-Response.

Here’s how the exploitation chain worked:

docs.title: Step 1: Execute a Command
docs.text:
@java.lang.Runtime@getRuntime().exec("whoami").getInputStream()

This executes the whoami command and captures the output as an InputStream.

docs.title: Step 2: Convert the Output
docs.text:
@org.apache.commons.io.IOUtils@toString(...,"utf-8")

This converts the InputStream to a UTF-8 String and stores it in a variable (let’s call it #a).

docs.title: Step 3: Exfiltrate via HTTP Header
docs.text:
@com.opensymphony.webwork.ServletActionContext@getResponse().setHeader("X-Cmd-Response", #a)

This accesses the HTTP Response object and adds a new header named X-Cmd-Response with the value containing the command output stored in #a.

All of this is wrapped in the OGNL format: ${...}

docs.title: The Complete Request Format
docs.text:
The HTTP response from the server would look something like this:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8
X-Cmd-Response: confluence

Using the same approach, any code that establishes a reverse shell would work just as effectively. 🙂

docs.title: Post-Exploitation: What Happened Next
docs.text: Once inside, attackers had their sights set on large enterprises. We all know where this is headed, but what exactly did they do with that user access?

docs.title: Real-World Exploitation: The Crypto Mining Campaign
docs.text:
One particularly notable exploitation campaign through this CVE involved sending malware payloads that downloaded shell script files named ro[.]sh and ap[.]sh, which subsequently established C2 (Command and Control) connections.

Through the C2 channel, attackers downloaded a cryptocurrency miner — malware designed to hijack system resources for mining cryptocurrency. The sophistication was impressive:

Initial Setup:

  • Disabled iptables (firewall rules) to maintain stealth
  • Downloaded PwnKit for privilege escalation
  • Loaded the ap[.]sh script, which disabled any competing malware on the system (how thoughtful! 🙄)

Lateral Movement:

  • Established SSH connections to spread across the network
  • Exploited additional hosts to maximize mining resources

Persistence Mechanisms:

  • If the host was Linux-based, the malware modified /etc/ld.so.preload (similar to Windows DLL files), allowing it to inject malware libraries into processes
  • Performed comprehensive hard disk scanning to identify additional exploitation opportunities

And that’s it — we finally made it through! 😅

docs.title: Detection: How to Identify This Attack
docs.text:
The primary detection method is examining HTTP logs that reveal suspicious requests containing OGNL patterns. Look for:

  • Unusual URI patterns with ${...} syntax
  • Requests to Confluence endpoints with embedded Java expressions
  • Custom headers like X-Cmd-Response in responses
  • Sudden outbound connections from Confluence servers

docs.title: The Patch: How Atlassian Fixed It
docs.text:
The remediation was straightforward but critical:

  1. Stopped translating any code within HTTP requests — preventing OGNL interpretation of user-controlled input
  2. Implemented filtering for suspicious requests — blocking patterns matching OGNL injection attempts

That’s it! Sometimes the simplest solutions are the most effective.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Patch immediately: Zero-day vulnerabilities like this demonstrate why emergency patching procedures are essential
  • Monitor HTTP logs: Your logs are your first line of defense for detecting exploitation attempts
  • Network segmentation: Limiting lateral movement can contain breaches even when initial compromise occurs
  • Assume breach: The window between disclosure and patching is a race against time

docs.title: Closing Thoughts
docs.text: And That Set إن أصبت فهو من عند الله و إن أخطأت فهو من نفسي و الشيطان :) Stay vigilant. Stay patched. Stay secure.

docs.title: How a Single Image in Your WhatsApp Could Have Owned Your iPhone
How a Single Image in Your WhatsApp Could Have Owned Your iPhone
docs.text:
A deep dive into CVE-2025–43300 — the Zero Click vulnerability hiding inside Apple’s image processing pipeline.

سبحان الذي علم بالقلم, علم الإنسان ما لم يعلم

We all know Zero Click vulnerabilities — the attack executes without the user doing literally anything. We hear stories and go “wow, they found a Zero Click!” Or some Zero Day drops and they say it’s Zero Click, then a thousand patch-your-OS warnings flood in. But how does this actually happen?

The most dangerous exploit is the one that requires zero interaction — you don’t click, you don’t open, you don’t know.

Last year’s scenario: CVE-2025–43300 — a Zero Click vulnerability on Apple systems. Through a crafted image sent to the victim, the attacker achieved an Out-of-Bounds Write in Memory. That’s a Buffer Overflow, which means Malicious process hollowing, for example. By the time you figure out who sent you the image — or that there even was an image — you’re already compromised.

docs.title: First, we need to understand a few things
docs.text:
Adobe created a Raw image format (camera raw files) called DNG. Inside a DNG, there’s compressed image info so you don’t lose detail (unlike JPEG lossy compression). The DNG structure has two critical sections:

SectionWhat it containsKey parameterTIFF MetadataImage information and parameters SamplesPerPixel — number of channels per pixel (e.g., RGB = 3 channels)JPEG StreamContains an SOF3 marker — image info used during decompression NumComponents — number of channels per pixel during decompression (the code reads this, not the metadata)

Important note: when the image gets decompressed, the code references the JPEG stream’s NumComponents — not the TIFF metadata. These two values are supposed to match. That mismatch is exactly where things get interesting.

docs.title: So where’s the vulnerability?
docs.text: In the library that processes and decompresses images: ImageIO. Inside it there’s a sublibrary called RawCamera.bundle — exists as a file inside the dyld_shared_cache on every Apple device. Inside that, there's a class called CDNGLosslessJpegUnpacker — the class responsible for decompressing Lossless JPEG inside DNG files.

docs.title: To reach the vulnerable function, you need to pass two check conditions:
docs.text:
Condition 1 field_d8 = (null) and field_dc = 2

field_d8 and field_dc are internal fields (variables) inside the CDNGLosslessJpegUnpacker class. They hold the unpacker's state. field_d8 points to a pointer or specific flag; field_dc holds the number of channels or tile type. These correspond to TIFF tags in the image metadata — so if the image follows the right structure, the condition passes automatically.

Condition 2A check on SamplesPerPixel and NumComponents.

First it allocates buffer space in Memory normally. Then: if (NumComponents != 2) → enters the vulnerable path else → normal code runs on the same allocated space, nothing wrong

docs.title: Okay, but where’s the actual attack?
docs.text:
Now we know the attacker needs to arrange TIFF tags in the image metadata to satisfy Condition 1 — that’s the easy part. For Condition 2, they need NumComponents != 2 in the decompressed data. The attacker sets it to 1 (one channel — grayscale).

Then they set SamplesPerPixel = 2 in the Metadata.

Wait — didn’t we say both represent the number of channels? Shouldn’t they always be the same value? Exactly. So the attacker writes in the metadata that the image is not grayscale (grayscale = 1 channel = 1 byte). By setting it to 2, they’re telling the parser this is one of the medical image types — and those calculate the channel as 2 bytes.

docs.title: Let’s walk through the math — simplified with a 1000×1 pixel image:
docs.text:
// Buffer allocation — uses SamplesPerPixel from Metadata 1000 pixels × 2 samples × 2 bytes = 4,000 bytes allocated ✓

// Enter the vulnerable condition: NumComponents = 1, so (NumComponents != 2) is true // Outer for loop runs: for (i = 1; i < 1000 × 2; i += 1) → 2000 iterations // Each iteration: pointer advances by 2 samples (pixel by pixel) // Total samples written: 2000 × 2 = 4000 samples // Each sample/channel = 2 bytes

4,000 samples × 2 bytes = 8,000 bytes written Allocated: 4,000 bytes → Written: 8,000 bytes

Out-of-Bounds Write: +4,000 bytes past the buffer boundary 💀

0x0000 ████████████████████ ← allocated buffer (4000 bytes) safe zone

0x0FA0 ████████████████████ ← end of safe zone

0x0FA0 ████████████████████ ← OVERFLOW BEGINS here

0x1F40 ████████████████████ ← +4000 bytes past boundary (arbitrary write)

↑ arbitrary code execution territory

That’s a Buffer Overflow → arbitrary code execution. And iMessage, which processes images automatically, is open by default on every iPhone.

And all of this happened because an image showed up in your messages. On WhatsApp. You didn’t tap it. You didn’t open it. You’re already compromised. :)

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text: Craft the malicious DNG imageSet TIFF tags to satisfy field_d8 = null and field_dc = 2. Set SamplesPerPixel = 2 in TIFF metadata (signals medical image type, 2 bytes per channel). Set NumComponents = 1 in the JPEG stream (signals grayscale to the decompressor).

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text: Deliver via any messaging appiMessage, WhatsApp, anything that auto-processes image previews. Zero user interaction required.

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text: ImageIO triggers automatically RawCamera.bundle → CDNGLosslessJpegUnpacker starts processing. Passes both conditions. Buffer allocated based on SamplesPerPixel = 2.

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text: Out-of-Bounds Write executesThe for loop writes 8,000 bytes into a 4,000 byte buffer. 4,000 bytes of overflow into adjacent memory regions. Arbitrary code execution achieved.

docs.title: Done
docs.text: Device compromised — silentlyYou never saw a prompt. You never tapped anything. You don’t even know who sent it.

docs.title: The patch — one line of code
docs.text:
Apple added a single condition check before the for loop:

if (NumComponents == SamplesPerPixel)

Before entering the vulnerable path, the parser now verifies that both values agree. If the JPEG stream says grayscale (1 channel) but the TIFF metadata says 2 samples per pixel — they don’t match, the check fails, execution stops. The mismatch that enabled the entire exploit is now explicitly caught.

One comparison. That’s it. That’s the entire fix for a complete device takeover.

docs.title: Was everyone compromised?
docs.text:
Yes — technically. But crafting the image or payload with all the right conditions without corrupting the image itself is genuinely difficult. That’s why this vulnerability was being exploited only against targeted individuals, not in mass campaigns. The barrier to weaponization was high enough that it couldn’t be sprayed at random.

Which, if you think about it, might be the scariest version: the people running this exploit were being very deliberate about who they used it on.

إن أصبت فهو من عند الله وإن أخطأت فهو من نفسي والشيطان :)

docs.title: Building a Security Monitoring Stack: Integrating Any Tool with Elasticsearch Using Docker
Building a Security Monitoring Stack: Integrating Any Tool with Elasticsearch Using Docker
docs.text:
A practical guide to connecting security tools like Suricata to Elasticsearch for unified monitoring

وما توفيقي إلا بالله :)

docs.title: The Universal Integration Pattern
docs.text: After integrating multiple security tools (Suricata, Packetbeat, OSQuery, and more) into my Elasticsearch stack, I noticed a repeating pattern. Here’s the framework that works for almost any tool:

docs.title: The 5-Step Integration Recipe
docs.text:
1. Tool Container    → Generates security data
2. Log Storage       → Persists the data (Docker volume)
3. Filebeat Shipper  → Reads logs and ships to Elasticsearch
4. Elasticsearch     → Indexes and stores events
5. Kibana Discover   → Visualizes and analyzes data

Let’s break down each step.

docs.title: Step 1: Understanding Docker Networking
docs.text:
The Foundation: Bridge Network

Before connecting any tools, you need a shared network where all containers can communicate.

# docker-compose.yml
networks:
  security-net:
    driver: bridge
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.19.0.0/16

What this does:

  • Creates an isolated network for your security stack
  • Assigns IPs automatically (172.19.0.2, 172.19.0.3, etc.)
  • Containers can reach each other by name (e.g., elasticsearch:9200)
  • Your monitoring tools can see each other’s traffic (important for network sensors!)

Key Insight: All your containers must be on the same network to communicate. This seems obvious but is the #1 issue I see beginners face.

docs.title: Step 2: Persistent Storage with Volumes
docs.text:
The Problem: Containers are ephemeral. When they restart, data is lost.

The Solution: Docker volumes provide persistent storage that survives container restarts.

volumes:
  elasticsearch-data:   # Stores your security events (critical!)
  suricata-logs:       # Stores Suricata's raw logs
  tool-logs:           # Generic pattern for any tool

Volume Types You’ll Use:

  1. Data Volumes (for Elasticsearch):

  2. Stores indexed events

  3. Location: Docker manages this (usually /var/lib/docker/volumes/)
  4. Critical: Deleting this = losing all your data!

2. Log Volumes (for tools):

  • Temporary storage for raw logs
  • Filebeat reads from here
  • Can be safely deleted (Elasticsearch has the data)

Best Practice: Always mount tool logs to a volume, even if you think you don’t need it. You’ll thank yourself during debugging.

docs.title: Step 3: The Tool Container — Common Patterns
docs.text: Every security tool container needs:

docs.title: A. Basic Container Configuration
docs.text:
your-tool:
  image: vendor/tool:version
  container_name: descriptive-name
  networks:
    - security-net
  volumes:
    - tool-logs:/var/log/tool
  restart: unless-stopped

docs.title: B. Tool-Specific Configurations
docs.text:
Some tools need special permissions or network modes:

Network Sensors (Suricata, Packetbeat):

cap_add:
  - NET_ADMIN    # Modify network configuration
  - NET_RAW      # Access raw packets
network_mode: "container:target"  # Share another container's network

Endpoint Agents (OSQuery):

volumes:
  - ./config.conf:/etc/tool/config.conf:ro  # Mount configuration
  - tool-logs:/var/log/tool                 # Log output
command: ["tool", "--config", "/etc/tool/config.conf"]

docs.title: C. Critical Configuration Requirements
docs.text:
Your tool MUST:

  1. Write logs to a known location (e.g., /var/log/tool/events.log)
  2. Use JSON format (Elasticsearch’s native format)
  3. Include timestamps in each event
  4. Flush logs immediately (don’t buffer for too long)

Example OSQuery Configuration:

{
  "options": {
    "logger_path": "/var/log/osquery",
    "logger_plugin": "filesystem",
    "log_result_events": "true"
  }
}

docs.title: Step 4: Filebeat — The Universal Shipper
docs.text:
Why Filebeat?

  • Lightweight (low resource usage)
  • Guaranteed delivery (retries on failure)
  • Handles backpressure (won’t overwhelm Elasticsearch)
  • Works with any log file

docs.title: The Generic Filebeat Pattern
docs.text:
tool-filebeat:
  image: docker.elastic.co/beats/filebeat:8.15.0
  container_name: tool-filebeat
  user: root
  volumes:
    - tool-logs:/var/log/tool:ro    # Read-only mount!
  networks:
    - security-net
  command: >
    bash -c "
      cat > /usr/share/filebeat/filebeat.yml <<'EOF'
      filebeat.inputs:
        - type: log
          enabled: true
          paths:
            - /var/log/tool/*.log
          json.keys_under_root: true
          json.add_error_key: true

      output.elasticsearch:
        hosts: ['elasticsearch:9200']
        index: 'tool-events-%{+yyyy.MM.dd}'

      setup.ilm.enabled: false
      setup.template.enabled: false
      EOF

      filebeat -e
    "
  depends_on:
    - elasticsearch
  restart: unless-stopped

docs.title: Key Filebeat Settings Explained
docs.text:
Input Configuration:

paths:
  - /var/log/tool/*.log    # Where to find logs

json.keys_under_root: true  # Flatten JSON (important!)
# Without this:
#   {"message": {"timestamp": "...", "alert": "..."}}
# With this:
#   {"timestamp": "...", "alert": "..."}json.add_error_key: true    # Track parsing errors

Output Configuration:

hosts: ['elasticsearch:9200']           # Container name + port
index: 'tool-events-%{+yyyy.MM.dd}'    # Daily indices
# Creates: tool-events-2024.01.30, tool-events-2024.01.31, etc.

Why daily indices?

  • Easier to delete old data
  • Better query performance
  • Simpler lifecycle management

docs.title: Step 5: Elasticsearch & Kibana Setup
docs.text:
Elasticsearch (The Storage Engine):

elasticsearch:
  image: docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.15.0
  container_name: elasticsearch
  environment:
    - discovery.type=single-node
    - xpack.security.enabled=false    # ⚠️ Dev only!
    - "ES_JAVA_OPTS=-Xms4g -Xmx4g"   # 4GB RAM
  ports:
    - "9200:9200"
  volumes:
    - elasticsearch-data:/usr/share/elasticsearch/data
  networks:
    - security-net
  restart: unless-stopped

Important Notes:

  • xpack.security.enabled=false is for development only
  • For production: Enable authentication, use HTTPS
  • RAM allocation: Set to 50% of available memory (max 32GB)

Kibana (The Interface):

kibana:
  image: docker.elastic.co/kibana/kibana:8.15.0
  container_name: kibana
  environment:
    - ELASTICSEARCH_HOSTS=http://elasticsearch:9200
  ports:
    - "5601:5601"
  networks:
    - security-net
  depends_on:
    - elasticsearch
  restart: unless-stopped

docs.title: Step 6: Kibana Data View & Discover Setup
docs.text: This is where many people get stuck. Here’s the correct process:

docs.title: Creating a Data View
docs.text:
1. Open Kibana:http://localhost:5601
  2. Navigate: Menu → Stack Management → Data Views
  3. Create Data View:
Name: Tool Events
   Index pattern: tool-events-*
   Timestamp field: @timestamp
  1. Common Issues:Problem: “No matching indices found”
# Check if data exists:
   curl http://localhost:9200/tool-events-*/_count

   # If count > 0 but Kibana doesn't see it:
   # Refresh the page and try again

Problem: “Could not locate time field”

Cause: Your logs don't have @timestamp field

   Solution: Add to Filebeat config:
     json.keys_under_root: true
     json.overwrite_keys: true

   Or add explicit timestamp processing

docs.title: Using Discover
docs.text:
Select Data View: Choose “Tool Events” from dropdown

Set Time Range:

  • Top right corner
  • Start with “Last 7 days”
  • Adjust based on your data

Add Useful Columns:

Common columns for security tools:
   - @timestamp
   - event.type
   - source.ip
   - destination.ip
   - alert.signature (for IDS)
   - message

Filter Data:

KQL Examples:
   - event.type: "alert"
   - source.ip: "192.168.1.50"
   - alert.severity: "high"
   - message: *SQL*injection*

docs.title: Challenge 1: Timestamp Issues
docs.text:
Problem: Events appear at wrong time or Kibana shows “No results”

Root Causes:

  1. Tool doesn’t include timestamp
  2. Timestamp format not recognized
  3. Timezone mismatch

Solutions:

# Filebeat: Add timestamp processing
processors:
  - timestamp:
      field: custom_timestamp
      target_field: "@timestamp"
      layouts:
        - '2006-01-02T15:04:05Z'
        - 'UNIX'

Or configure tool to use ISO 8601 format:

2024-01-30T15:23:45.123Z  ✅ Good
1706626425                ✅ Unix timestamp (also good)
30/01/2024 15:23:45       ❌ Ambiguous

docs.title: Challenge 2: Data Not Appearing
docs.text:
Debugging Checklist:

# 1. Check if tool is running
docker ps | grep tool-name

# 2. Check if logs are being written
docker exec tool-container ls -lh /var/log/tool/# 3. Check if Filebeat sees the logs
docker logs tool-filebeat | grep "Harvester started"# 4. Check if Elasticsearch received data
curl http://localhost:9200/tool-events-*/_count# 5. Check Filebeat registry
docker exec tool-filebeat cat /usr/share/filebeat/data/registry/filebeat/log.json

docs.title: Challenge 3: Container Communication Failures
docs.text:
Problem: Filebeat can’t reach Elasticsearch

Common Causes:

# ❌ Wrong: Using localhost
hosts: ['localhost:9200']

# ❌ Wrong: Using host IP in container
hosts: ['192.168.1.100:9200']# ✅ Correct: Using container name
hosts: ['elasticsearch:9200']

How to verify connectivity:

# From inside Filebeat container:
docker exec tool-filebeat curl http://elasticsearch:9200

# Should return Elasticsearch version info

docs.title: Real-World Example: Integrating Suricata IDS
docs.text: Now let’s see the complete pattern in action with Suricata, a popular network intrusion detection system.

docs.title: Step 1: Suricata Container
docs.text:
suricata:
  image: jasonish/suricata:latest
  container_name: suricata-ids
  cap_add:
    - NET_ADMIN
    - NET_RAW
  network_mode: "container:target-container"
  volumes:
    - suricata-logs:/var/log/suricata
  restart: unless-stopped

Key Points:

  • cap_add: Required for packet capture
  • network_mode: Attaches to another container's network interface
  • Logs written to: /var/log/suricata/eve.json

docs.title: Step 2: Suricata Filebeat
docs.text:
suricata-filebeat:
  image: docker.elastic.co/beats/filebeat:8.15.0
  container_name: suricata-filebeat
  user: root
  volumes:
    - suricata-logs:/var/log/suricata:ro
  networks:
    - security-net
  command: >
    bash -c "
      cat > /usr/share/filebeat/filebeat.yml <<'EOF'
      filebeat.inputs:
        - type: log
          enabled: true
          paths:
            - /var/log/suricata/eve.json
          json.keys_under_root: true
          json.add_error_key: true
          fields:
            log_type: suricata
            sensor: ids-001
          fields_under_root: true

      output.elasticsearch:
        hosts: ['elasticsearch:9200']
        index: 'suricata-%{+yyyy.MM.dd}'

      setup.ilm.enabled: false
      setup.template.enabled: false

      logging.level: info
      logging.to_stderr: true
      EOF

      filebeat -e
    "
  depends_on:
    - elasticsearch
  restart: unless-stopped

Additional Fields Explained:

fields:
  log_type: suricata    # Identify source
  sensor: ids-001       # Identify specific sensor
fields_under_root: true  # Don't nest under "fields"

docs.title: Step 3: Elasticsearch & Kibana (Same as before)
docs.text:
elasticsearch:
  # ... (same configuration as shown earlier)

kibana:
  # ... (same configuration as shown earlier)

docs.title: Step 4: Verification
docs.text:
Check Suricata Logs:

# View raw logs
docker exec suricata-ids tail -f /var/log/suricata/eve.json

# Should see JSON events like:
{
  "timestamp": "2024-01-30T15:23:45.123456+0000",
  "event_type": "alert",
  "src_ip": "192.168.1.50",
  "dest_ip": "172.19.0.5",
  "alert": {
    "signature": "ET EXPLOIT SQL Injection Attempt",
    "severity": 1
  }
}

Check Filebeat Shipping:

docker logs suricata-filebeat

# Look for:
# "Harvester started for file: /var/log/suricata/eve.json"
# "Non-zero metrics in the last period"

Query Elasticsearch:

# Count events
curl http://localhost:9200/suricata-*/_count

# Get sample event
curl http://localhost:9200/suricata-*/_search?size=1 | jq

docs.title: Step 5: Kibana Data View
docs.text:
Create Data View:

Name: Suricata IDS Events
Index pattern: suricata-*
Timestamp: @timestamp

Essential Columns in Discover:

  • @timestamp
  • event_type
  • src_ip
  • dest_ip
  • alert.signature
  • alert.severity

Useful Queries:

# High severity alerts
alert.severity: 1

# Specific attack type
alert.signature: *SQL*injection*# Source IP
src_ip: "192.168.1.50"# Time range + filter
@timestamp >= "2024-01-30" AND event_type: "alert"

docs.title: Step 6: Results
docs.text:
After everything is running, you should see:

In Elasticsearch:

$ curl http://localhost:9200/suricata-*/_count
{"count": 45519}  # My actual results!

In Kibana Discover:

2,471 documents found
(showing events from last 7 days)

Sample event:
@timestamp: Jan 30, 2024 @ 19:05:29.622
src_ip: 172.19.0.8
dest_ip: 172.19.0.5
alert.signature: ET EXPLOIT SQL Injection SELECT FROM
alert.severity: 1
event_type: alert

docs.title: Troubleshooting Flowchart
docs.text:
Data not appearing in Kibana?
    │
    ├─> Is tool container running?
    │   └─> No: Check docker logs, fix configuration
    │   └─> Yes: Continue
    │
    ├─> Are logs being written?
    │   └─> docker exec tool ls -lh /var/log/tool/
    │   └─> No: Check tool configuration
    │   └─> Yes: Continue
    │
    ├─> Is Filebeat reading logs?
    │   └─> docker logs filebeat | grep "Harvester started"
    │   └─> No: Check paths, permissions
    │   └─> Yes: Continue
    │
    ├─> Is data in Elasticsearch?
    │   └─> curl http://localhost:9200/index-*/_count
    │   └─> No: Check Filebeat connection, credentials
    │   └─> Yes: Continue
    │
    └─> Data view configured correctly?
        └─> Check index pattern, timestamp field
        └─> Refresh field list

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Integrating security tools with Elasticsearch via Docker follows a consistent pattern:

  1. Network: Shared bridge network for communication
  2. Volumes: Persistent storage for data and logs
  3. Tool Container: Generates security events
  4. Filebeat: Ships logs reliably to Elasticsearch
  5. Data View: Makes data visible in Kibana

Once you understand this pattern, you can integrate almost any security tool in 30–60 minutes.

وبس كدا ان اصبت فهو من عند الله وان اخطأت فهو من نفسي والشيطان :)

docs.title: Findcrypt3 IDA Plugin
docs.text: Unlocking Hidden Secrets: A Malware Analyst’s Journey with FindCrypt3 Plugin

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: In the world of malware analysis, identifying cryptographic routines embedded in malware is crucial for extracting hidden configurations, decrypting payloads, and understanding the malware’s operational intent. One powerful tool in a malware analyst’s arsenal is the FindCrypt3 plugin for IDA Pro. This article details my experience downloading, configuring, and testing the FindCrypt3 plugin, along with the challenges faced and how I overcame them. Additionally, I will highlight the tangible benefits that this plugin offers for malware analysis.

docs.title: Downloading and Installing FindCrypt3
docs.text:
The journey began with downloading the FindCrypt3 plugin, an IDA Pro extension designed to identify hardcoded cryptographic constants (such as AES S-Boxes) in malware binaries. The plugin can be found in public GitHub repositories or through IDA community sources.

Steps to Download:

  1. Navigate to the FindCrypt3 GitHub repository.
  2. Clone the repository using:
git clone https://github.com/polymorf/findcrypt3.git
  1. Alternatively, download the ZIP file and extract it to your desired directory.

Installation Process:

  1. Copy the extracted findcrypt3.py and findcrypt3.rules files to the IDA Pro plugin directory (usually located at C:\Program Files\IDA Pro\plugins).
  2. Ensure the file structure resembles:
C:\Program Files\IDA Pro\plugins\findcrypt3.py
C:\Program Files\IDA Pro\plugins\findcrypt3.rules
  • Restart IDA Pro to load the new plugin.

docs.title: Errors Encountered and Solutions
docs.text:
1. Python Configuration Error: Upon launching IDA Pro, I was greeted with the following error:

WARNING: Python 3 is not configured (Python3TargetDLL value is not set).
Please run idapyswitch to select a Python 3 install.

Solution:

  • Download and install Python 3 from python.org.
  • Make sure it the verision suitable for ida verision.
  • Run the following command to set the Python path:
idapyswitch.exe
  • Choose the Python 3 executable path when prompted.

2. Invalid Win32 Application Error: Another issue occurred when IDA attempted to load idapython3.dll:

LoadLibrary(C:\Program Files\IDA Pro\plugins\idapython3.dll) error: %1 is not a valid Win32 application.

Solution:

  • This error indicated a mismatch between the plugin’s architecture and IDA Pro’s version (32-bit vs 64-bit).
  • I ensured the correct Python version (64-bit) was installed, matching the 64-bit version of IDA Pro.
  • Reinstalled the correct idapython3.dll and placed it in the plugins directory.

3. YARA Module Not Found Error: Running the plugin revealed another issue:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "C:\Program Files\IDA Pro\plugins\findcrypt3.py", line 9, in <module>
    import yara
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yara'

Solution:

  • Installed the yara-python module:
pip install yara-python
  • Restarted IDA Pro, resolving the missing module issue.

docs.title: Testing the Plugin
docs.text:
With FindCrypt3 successfully installed, I proceeded to test the plugin by analyzing a suspected malware sample.

Test Case: I analyzed a simple C program that includes the AES S-Box to test the findcrypt-yara plugin in IDA Pro. This binary will contain known cryptographic constants that findcrypt-yara should detect.

docs.title: 3. Load in IDA Pro
